title: In-Class Exercise 4
text:
Contiguity-based neighbours
poly2nb() derives neighbours directly from the polygon topology. Under the queen rule, counties are neighbours when their boundaries share either an edge or a corner. The stricter rook rule requires a shared edge.


Show the R code
queen_nb <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE, row.names = hunan$County)
rook_nb <- poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE, row.names = hunan$County)

neighbour_summary <- function(nb, method) {
  counts <- card(nb)
  data.frame(
    Method = method,
    `Directed links` = sum(counts),
    `Average neighbours` = round(mean(counts), 2),
    `Minimum neighbours` = min(counts),
    `Maximum neighbours` = max(counts),
    `Connected components` = n.comp.nb(nb)$nc,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

contiguity_summary <- bind_rows(
  neighbour_summary(queen_nb, "Queen contiguity"),
  neighbour_summary(rook_nb, "Rook contiguity")
)

title: In-Class Exercise 4
text:
Distance-based neighbours
Contiguity may not represent every kind of interaction. The chapter therefore introduces two distance-based alternatives. I retain its 62 km fixed band, which gives every county at least one neighbour and keeps the province in a single connected component. I also construct a six-nearest-neighbour graph, which gives every county the same number of outgoing links.


Show the R code
distance_62_nb <- dnearneigh(
  coords,
  d1 = 0,
  d2 = 62,
  row.names = hunan$County,
  longlat = TRUE
)

knn6_nb <- knn2nb(
  knearneigh(coords, k = 6, longlat = TRUE),
  row.names = hunan$County
)

distance_summary <- bind_rows(
  neighbour_summary(distance_62_nb, "Fixed distance: 62 km"),
  neighbour_summary(knn6_nb, "Six nearest neighbours")
)

title: In-Class Exercise 4
text:
From neighbours to weights
A neighbour list only records who is connected. nb2listw() assigns numeric weights to those links. Binary weights give every neighbour a value of 1. Row-standardised weights divide each row by its number of neighbours, so the weights for each county add to 1. Inverse-distance weights give closer neighbours more influence before the same row standardisation is applied.


Show the R code
queen_binary <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
queen_row <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

queen_distances <- nbdists(queen_nb, coords, longlat = TRUE)
inverse_distance <- lapply(queen_distances, function(x) 1 / x)
queen_idw <- nb2listw(
  queen_nb,
  glist = inverse_distance,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

anxiang_weights <- data.frame(
  County = hunan$County[anxiang_neighbour_ids],
  `Distance (km)` = round(queen_distances[[anxiang_id]], 1),
  Binary = queen_binary$weights[[anxiang_id]],
  `Row-standardised` = round(queen_row$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),
  `Row-standardised inverse distance` = round(queen_idw$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  arrange(County)

title: In-Class Exercise 4
text:
Spatially lagged GDPPC
The spatial lag is the weighted combination of neighbouring values. With row-standardised queen weights, it is the mean GDPPC among a county’s neighbours.


Show the R code
hunan$lag_gdppc <- lag.listw(
  queen_row,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$neighbour_sum <- lag.listw(
  queen_binary,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

queen_self_nb <- include.self(queen_nb)
queen_self_row <- nb2listw(queen_self_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
queen_self_binary <- nb2listw(queen_self_nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)

hunan$window_average <- lag.listw(
  queen_self_row,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$window_sum <- lag.listw(
  queen_self_binary,
  hunan$GDPPC,
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

hunan$own_minus_lag <- hunan$GDPPC - hunan$lag_gdppc

lag_examples <- hunan |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(
    County,
    GDPPC,

Geographically weighted summary statistics
GWmodel still expects an older Spatial object for these functions, so I convert the joined sf object only at this point. The main data object remains in sf format for importing, joining, mapping and spatial weights.
The adaptive bandwidth is selected by leave-one-out cross-validation with bw.gwr(). I use the local regression GDPPC ~ GIO + Agri + Service because those four measures were retained during data preparation. The returned bandwidth is a neighbour count, not a distance in kilometres. I then use the same adaptive bisquare kernel for the local summary statistics.

title: In-Class Exercise 4
text:
Assumptions and limits

A queen link assumes that any shared edge or corner can support interaction. A different substantive process may call for rook, road-network or travel-time neighbours.
The distance methods use polygon centroids. Large or irregular counties are reduced to one representative point, and the 62 km threshold is a connectivity rule rather than an economic boundary.
Six-nearest-neighbour links impose equal outgoing neighbour counts even where settlement density differs. They can also be asymmetric.
Row standardisation gives every county the same total weight, which increases the individual influence of neighbours around counties with few links.
GDPPC is a county-level, cross-sectional indicator. A spatial lag describes context; it does not show that neighbouring GDPPC caused a county’s value.
The adaptive bandwidth is selected for the GWR equation and then reused for the summary statistics. A bandwidth chosen for a different equation could produce a different local pattern.
GWmodel requires the temporary conversion from sf to Spatial. Row order is preserved during the conversion and checked before the GWSS results are attached.

title: In-Class Exercise 4
text:
What I found
Changing the neighbour rule changes the graph, even though the 88 county values stay the same. I use queen contiguity as the main specification because the question concerns counties that touch. With row-standardised weights, each spatial lag is the mean among those neighbours. Lengshuijiang, Changsha and Zixing are well above their surrounding averages, while Pingjiang is well below. The geographically weighted mean and median add a broader regional view, using an adaptive bandwidth selected by cross-validation. All of these results are descriptive. They do not show that one county’s GDPPC caused another’s.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Technical Report
text:
Road accidents occur at specific places and times, making point-pattern methods suitable for studying their distribution. The dataset contains 3,597 distinct accident events recorded in 2022 within a six-province Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR). I examine where and when those records concentrate and whether nearby events remain unusually common after allowing for broad variation in intensity.
The unit of analysis is a recorded accident location. Traffic volume, road length, vehicle kilometres travelled, road design and enforcement exposure are unavailable, so the results cannot estimate exposure-adjusted accident risk. Areas with many records may simply carry more traffic or contain more mapped roads.



How did the spatial and temporal intensity of recorded BMR road accidents vary during 2022?
Does the point pattern show interaction beyond broad first-order intensity, and at what distances?
For the bonus analysis, were spatially close accidents also unusually close in time after preserving the observed spatial and temporal margins?




I first audit the source data and construct the study window. I then compare temporal and spatial intensity, test complete spatial randomness (CSR) and an inhomogeneous null model, examine bandwidth sensitivity, and apply a Monte Carlo Knox test for space-time interaction.

2.2 Spatial study window
The BMR is operationalised as Bangkok, Samut Prakan, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom and Samut Sakhon. This matches the grouping used by Thailand’s National Statistical Office. The six ADM1 polygons form a 7,604.1 km² observation window.

2.3 Point-event definition
One point represents one reported accident occurrence. The temporal field is incident_datetime; the spatial fields are longitude and latitude. Two pairs of rows had different accident codes but the same incident time, coordinates, agency, route, accident type and casualty totals. I treat each pair as one event and retain the earlier record. Events at identical coordinates remain separate when their timestamps differ because they may represent recurrent accidents at the same recorded location.
Records enter the analysis when they have a valid 2022 incident time, complete coordinates within plausible Thailand bounds, and a point inside the union of the six BMR polygons. Coordinates determine inclusion. Ten records labelled as Ayutthaya, Kanchanaburi or unknown fall inside the BMR boundary and are retained.

4.3 Kernel intensity estimate
Kernel density estimation (KDE) smooths event locations into an estimated intensity surface. I use a Gaussian kernel, 500 m output grid, edge correction and a 3 km primary bandwidth. Likelihood cross-validation selected approximately 751 m, but the resulting surface is fragmented and dominated by road-constrained points and repeated coordinates. I chose 3 km because the planning question concerns broad concentrations, then compare it with 2 km and 6 km estimates.

  geom_raster(
    data = kde_3km_df,
    aes(x, y, fill = events_per_km2)

  geom_sf(data = bmr_provinces_utm, fill = NA, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", direction = -1) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +

    subtitle = "Gaussian KDE, 3 km bandwidth, 500 m grid and edge correction",
    fill = "Estimated annual\nevents per km²",
    caption = "Intensity is a smoothed count surface, not exposure-adjusted risk."

    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = palette_main["navy"]),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#5b677a")

The 3 km surface reaches 5.7 estimated annual events per km² and places the broadest high-intensity zone across Bangkok, extending east towards Samut Prakan. Smaller concentrations follow developed corridors in the surrounding provinces. The kernel is evaluated in planar space even though crashes occur on roads. It therefore smooths across locations that may not be connected by the road network and should not be used to select an individual junction without finer road and exposure data.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Technical Report
text:
5.1 Research question and test design
The second-order question is whether accidents retain more neighbours within 0-15 km than expected after broad intensity variation is represented. I use the transformed L-function, \(L(r)-r\), because zero is the theoretical reference under a Poisson process. Positive departures indicate more neighbours within distance \(r\) than the null predicts; negative departures indicate fewer.
I compare two null models:

CSR: 99 simulations place the observed number of events uniformly within the BMR. It supplies a simple benchmark, although uneven roads and activity make uniform intensity unrealistic.
Inhomogeneous Poisson: 99 simulations draw the observed event count from a fixed 6 km pilot intensity. Broad first-order variation is retained while events remain independent conditional on intensity.

Both tests use 0-15 km at 250 m intervals, translation edge correction, WGS 84 / UTM 47N and pointwise 95% simulation envelopes. A maximum-standardised-deviation statistic supplies a global Monte Carlo test. Conditioning on event count prevents total-count variation from dominating the comparison.

    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#6b7280", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = observed_minus_r / 1000), colour = palette_main["red"], linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~model, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 15, by = 3)) +
  labs(

    subtitle = "Red: observed pattern; grey: pointwise 95% simulation envelope",
    x = "Distance r (km)",
    y = "L(r) - r (km)"

Observed L(r)-r compared with pointwise 95% envelopes under CSR and an inhomogeneous Poisson null.




CSR is rejected by the global deviation test (\(p\) = 0.01), and the observed curve lies above the envelope from 0.25 km through 15 km. A dense-looking map alone would not establish this departure; the simulated reference provides the comparison.
The inhomogeneous null is also rejected (\(p\) = 0.01). The observed curve is above the envelope from 0.25 to 14.50 km. The broad first-order trend therefore does not account for all of the excess neighbouring events. The result may also reflect road-network support, shared coordinates or a pilot surface that is too smooth to represent every relevant component of intensity.

Geoprocessing

Question 1: How much land is within 5 m of a cycling path?
A five-metre buffer is created on both sides of every cycling-path feature. Summing the separate buffer areas double-counts overlaps, so I also dissolve the buffers with st_union() to obtain the unique footprint.

  st_area() |>

)

title: Hands-on Exercise 1a
text:
What I found

The current official spatial files contain 323 subzones, 8,523 cycling-path features, and 2,290 pre-school locations.
Transforming from WGS84 to EPSG:3414 is essential before calculating metres or square kilometres.
The unique five-metre cycling-path buffer covers about 431.51 hectares.
TAMPINES EAST has the most pre-schools (72), while CECIL has the highest density (35.6 per km²).
Count and density answer different questions, and density is sensitive to very small subzone areas.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1a
text:
Limitations
The datasets come from different reference dates, so I treat this as a methods exercise rather than a fully time-aligned planning study. A five-metre buffer measures geometric proximity, not construction feasibility or legal land acquisition. Density per land area also does not account for the number or age of children living in each subzone.

Contiguity-based neighbours

    `Minimum neighbours` = min(counts),
    `Maximum neighbours` = max(counts),
    `Connected components` = n.comp.nb(nb)$nc,
    check.names = FALSE

text:
From neighbours to weights
A neighbour list only records who is connected. nb2listw() assigns numeric weights to those links. Binary weights give every neighbour a value of 1. Row-standardised weights divide each row by its number of neighbours, so the weights for each county add to 1. Inverse-distance weights give closer neighbours more influence before the same row standardisation is applied.


Show the R code
queen_binary <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
queen_row <- nb2listw(queen_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

inverse_distance <- lapply(queen_distances, function(x) 1 / x)
queen_idw <- nb2listw(
  queen_nb,
  glist = inverse_distance,
  style = "W",
  zero.policy = TRUE
)

anxiang_weights <- data.frame(
  County = hunan$County[anxiang_neighbour_ids],
  `Distance (km)` = round(queen_distances[[anxiang_id]], 1),
  Binary = queen_binary$weights[[anxiang_id]],
  `Row-standardised` = round(queen_row$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),
  `Row-standardised inverse distance` = round(queen_idw$weights[[anxiang_id]], 3),

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
Assumptions and limits

A queen link assumes that any shared edge or corner can support interaction. A different substantive process may call for rook, road-network or travel-time neighbours.
The distance methods use polygon centroids. Large or irregular counties are reduced to one representative point, and the 62 km threshold is a connectivity rule rather than an economic boundary.
Six-nearest-neighbour links impose equal outgoing neighbour counts even where settlement density differs. They can also be asymmetric.
Row standardisation gives every county the same total weight, which increases the individual influence of neighbours around counties with few links.
GDPPC is a county-level, cross-sectional indicator. A spatial lag describes context; it does not show that neighbouring GDPPC caused a county’s value.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4
text:
What I found
Changing the neighbour rule changes the graph, even though the 88 county values stay the same. I use queen contiguity as the main specification because the question concerns counties that touch. With row-standardised weights, each spatial lag is the mean among those neighbours. Most nearby counties have similar GDPPC, but Lengshuijiang, Changsha and Zixing are well above their surrounding averages, while Pingjiang is well below. These comparisons are descriptive; they do not show that one county’s GDPPC caused another’s.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2b
text:
What the four functions test

G-function: nearest-neighbour distances from events; an observed curve above CSR suggests unusually short event-to-event distances.
F-function: distances from empty locations to the nearest event; an observed curve below CSR suggests larger gaps between clusters.
K-function: cumulative event interaction over distance; values above CSR suggest clustering.
L-function: a variance-stabilised transformation of K; values above CSR again suggest clustering.

For each statistic, I run 99 CSR simulations to form a pointwise envelope. A fixed seed makes the result reproducible. This is an exploratory test; a confirmatory analysis should use more simulations and a global envelope.


Show the R code
set.seed(608)
nsim <- 99

make_envelopes <- function(x) {
  list(
    G = envelope(x, Gest, nsim = nsim, correction = "best", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    F = envelope(x, Fest, nsim = nsim, correction = "best", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    K = envelope(x, Kest, nsim = nsim, correction = "iso", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE),
    L = envelope(x, Lest, nsim = nsim, correction = "iso", rank = 1, verbose = FALSE)
  )
}

summarise_envelope <- function(e, direction) {

    `First departure (m)` = if (any(departure)) round(min(e$r[valid][departure])) else NA_real_,

Both planning areas depart from the CSR envelopes over meaningful distance ranges. The departure is stronger and more consistent in Tampines. G and F describe the nearest-event and empty-space components, while K and L show that the pattern persists across broader distances.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Spatio-temporal kernel density
The chapter uses spattemp.density(). I implement the same product-kernel idea directly: each monthly slice combines a 12 km Gaussian spatial kernel with a one-month Gaussian temporal kernel. I rescale values to 0–1 across all six slices so changes in the location and strength of concentrations can be compared.


Show the R code
province_window <- as.owin(st_union(province))
fire_xy <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)

fire_ppp <- ppp(
  x = fire_xy[, 1],
  y = fire_xy[, 2],
  window = province_window,
  checkdup = FALSE
)

target_months <- 7:12
spatial_bandwidth <- 12000
temporal_bandwidth <- 1

monthly_surfaces <- lapply(target_months, function(target_month) {
  temporal_weight <- dnorm(
    (fires$Month_num - target_month) / temporal_bandwidth
  )

  surface <- density(
    fire_ppp,
    sigma = spatial_bandwidth,
    weights = temporal_weight,
    edge = TRUE,
    dimyx = 110
  )

  as.data.frame(surface) |>
    mutate(Month = factor(month.abb[target_month], levels = month.abb[target_months]))
}) |>
  bind_rows()

monthly_surfaces <- monthly_surfaces |>
  mutate(Relative_intensity = value / max(value, na.rm = TRUE))




Show the R code
ggplot(monthly_surfaces, aes(x, y, fill = Relative_intensity)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = districts, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.15, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Month, ncol = 3) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(province), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", limits = c(0, 1), na.value = NA) +

  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )





Product-kernel space-time intensity slices, July–December 2023




Activity is already visible on Bangka Island in July. It becomes stronger across western and southern Bangka in August and September, then reaches its broadest and strongest concentration in Bangka Selatan in October. Intensity falls in November and contracts sharply by December.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Are space and time independent?
If space and time are independent, randomly reassigning dates to the observed locations should leave the number of near-space/near-time pairs broadly unchanged. I test this by permuting dates:

a spatial pair is “near” when locations are within 10 km;
a temporal pair is “near” when detections are within seven days;
dates are permuted among fixed locations 199 times.

This tests the same independence question as a space-time K-function while keeping the result concise and directly interpretable.


Show the R code
spatial_distance <- as.matrix(dist(fire_xy))
date_number <- as.integer(fires$acq_date)
upper_pairs <- upper.tri(spatial_distance)
near_in_space <- upper_pairs & spatial_distance <= 10000

count_close_pairs <- function(dates) {
  temporal_distance <- abs(outer(dates, dates, "-"))
  sum(near_in_space & temporal_distance <= 7)
}

observed_pairs <- count_close_pairs(date_number)

set.seed(608)
permuted_pairs <- replicate(
  199,
  count_close_pairs(sample(date_number))
)

permutation_p <- (1 + sum(permuted_pairs >= observed_pairs)) / (length(permuted_pairs) + 1)
pair_ratio <- observed_pairs / mean(permuted_pairs)

test_result <- data.frame(
  `Observed close pairs` = observed_pairs,
  `Mean under permutation` = round(mean(permuted_pairs), 1),
  `Observed / expected` = round(pair_ratio, 2),
  `Monte Carlo p-value` = permutation_p,
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(test_result, caption = "Space-time permutation test: 10 km and 7 days")

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
section: What I found and its limits
text:
What I found and its limits
1. Are location and time independent? No. The observed data contain 1831 close space-time pairs, 1.87 times the permutation expectation, with (p=) 0.005. Dates and locations therefore show significant interaction at the chosen 10 km / 7-day scale.
2. Where and when is clustering strongest? The largest annual and monthly concentration occurs in Bangka Selatan, peaking in October. The temporal KDE peaks around 11 October, and the space-time density surfaces show the hotspot expanding from July through October before receding.
NASA FIRMS records satellite detections, not verified fire incidents or burned area. Cloud cover, satellite revisit timing, duplicate detections of one fire, confidence, and the chosen bandwidths all affect the pattern. The analysis identifies space-time concentration; it does not establish ignition causes.

text:
Clark–Evans nearest-neighbour test
The null hypothesis is CSR. A Clark–Evans ratio below 1 means that nearest-neighbour distances are shorter than expected under CSR; a ratio above 1 points to a more regular pattern. I use the CDF edge correction because the Singapore window is not rectangular.


Show the R code
ce_sg <- clarkevans.test(
  childcare_ppp,
  correction = "cdf",
  alternative = "clustered"
)

ce_result <- data.frame(
  Area = "Singapore",
  `Clark-Evans R` = round(unname(ce_sg$statistic), 3),
  `p-value` = format.pval(ce_sg$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  Decision = ifelse(ce_sg$p.value < 0.05, "Reject CSR", "Do not reject CSR"),
  check.names = FALSE
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 2a
text:
Kernel density estimation
I let bw.diggle() select the fixed bandwidth from the data. I also estimate an adaptive KDE, which uses narrower kernels where points are dense and wider kernels in sparse areas. Both surfaces are expressed as estimated centres per square kilometre.


Show the R code
fixed_bandwidth <- bw.diggle(childcare_ppp)

fixed_kde <- density(
  childcare_ppp,
  sigma = fixed_bandwidth,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

adaptive_kde <- adaptive.density(
  childcare_ppp,
  f = 0.15,
  edge = TRUE,
  dimyx = 180
)

fixed_grid <- as.data.frame(fixed_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = paste0("Fixed KDE (h = ", round(fixed_bandwidth), " m)"))

adaptive_grid <- as.data.frame(adaptive_kde) |>
  mutate(value = value * 1e6, Method = "Adaptive KDE")

kde_grid <- bind_rows(fixed_grid, adaptive_grid)




Show the R code

  geom_raster() +
  geom_sf(data = planning_area, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth = 0.08, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs(planning_area), datum = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", trans = "sqrt", na.value = NA) +

KDE measures the concentration of facilities, not accessibility or whether demand is being met.

Brief at a glance
The official exercise brief requires six connected tasks:

The bonus analysis must answer a useful geospatial question beyond the core requirements. A new package or decorative visualisation alone does not meet the bonus standard.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Selected study design
The analysis uses Option B: Thailand road accidents in 2022. Event records come from the Thailand Road Accident 2019-2022 dataset, while provincial boundaries come from geoBoundaries Thailand ADM1.
I define the Bangkok Metropolitan Region as Bangkok, Samut Prakan, Nonthaburi, Pathum Thani, Nakhon Pathom and Samut Sakhon. Thailand’s National Statistical Office uses this six-province grouping. Distance and area calculations use WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647).

title: Take-home Exercise 1
text:
Analytical coverage

The data audit traces 81,735 raw records to 3,597 analysed events and documents missing coordinates, spatial filtering, province mismatches and duplicate handling.
First-order analysis compares monthly and hourly patterns, provincial event density and edge-corrected KDE at 2 km, 3 km and 6 km bandwidths.
Second-order analysis uses transformed L-functions, translation edge correction and 99 conditional simulations under CSR and an inhomogeneous Poisson model.
Sensitivity checks compare KDE bandwidths and repeat the inhomogeneous test after removing repeated coordinates.
The bonus applies a 199-run Monte Carlo Knox test at three space-time thresholds.
Fixed URLs, source-file checksums, scripts, parameters, a simulation seed and session information document the workflow.
